title: Sandakphu trek on the Singalila ridge: route, rules and costs
summary: The Sandakphu trek climbs from Manebhanjan at about 2,150 m along the Singalila ridge to Sandakphu at 3,636 m in three days, with views of Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse and Makalu. You must trek with a licensed guide, pay the Singalila National Park fee and carry ID; the best months are October to mid-December and March to May.
meta_description: Sandakphu trek guide: Singalila National Park guide rules, permits and ID, day-by-day route from Manebhanjan, costs, best months, kit and altitude advice.

sections.heading: Sandakphu at a glance
paras: Sandakphu is the highest point of the Singalila ridge and of West Bengal, at 3,636 m. The ridge runs north from Manebhanjan, about 28 km west of Darjeeling, along the border between India and Nepal, and most of the Indian side lies within Singalila National Park. The park was declared a wildlife sanctuary in 1986 and a national park in 1992.

From the summit you can see four of the five highest mountains in the world: Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse and Makalu. The whole Kangchenjunga range lies across the northern horizon, its outline often called the Sleeping Buddha. Few places in the Himalaya offer this view after such a short and moderate walk.

The trek is graded moderate. The classic route covers about 32 km from Manebhanjan to Sandakphu over three days, staying in family lodges at Tumling and Kalipokhri. You can return the same way, drive down by Land Rover, descend via Srikhola to Rimbik, or continue 21 km north to Phalut before descending. Most itineraries take five to seven days from Darjeeling and back.

sections.heading: Rules, permits and guides
paras: There is no special trekking permit for Sandakphu, but there are rules, and they change from time to time. Check current status before you travel. The key points at the time of writing are as follows.

The guide rule is the one that surprises people. Independent trekking without a guide is not allowed in the park. Guides are licensed by the forest department and the Manebhanjan guide association, and they rotate through a queue at the office. You can also book a guide in advance through a registered Darjeeling trekking operator, who will arrange the same licensed guides. A guide can lead a small group, so trekkers often team up at Manebhanjan to share the cost.
list: Every trekker must be accompanied by a licensed guide, hired at Manebhanjan or through a registered operator.
Everyone pays the Singalila National Park entry fee at the Manebhanjan check post, with extra fees for cameras. Foreigners pay a higher fee than Indians.
Carry original photo ID throughout: a passport, voter ID or Aadhaar card for Indians, and a passport with a valid Indian visa for foreigners.
Parts of the route, including Tumling and Jaubari, are in Nepal. Border posts may check ID, and you should not stray off the main trail.
The park traditionally closes to trekkers from mid-June to mid-September for the monsoon. Vehicles may still use the ridge track in some periods.
Littering is prohibited. Carry back all plastic and packaging, and use lodge toilets.

sections.heading: The route day by day
paras: The table shows the classic route with the Srikhola descent, which is what most first-time trekkers walk. Distances are approximate, because the path switches between old trails and the jeep track and guides choose shortcuts depending on conditions. Walking times are for a steady pace with breaks.

Day one is the hardest climb, from Manebhanjan past Chitrey monastery to Tumling. Day two is longer but gentler, through Jaubari and down to Gairibas before a long climb through bamboo and rhododendron to the small lake at Kalipokhri. Day three is short and steep, reaching Sandakphu before the clouds rise. Day four starts with sunrise on the summit and drops steeply through Gurdum to the river at Srikhola, and on day five a short walk takes you to Rimbik for a jeep back to Darjeeling.

sections.heading: When to go
paras: October to mid-December is the best time for views. The monsoon has washed the air clean, mornings are usually clear and the weather is stable, though nights at Sandakphu fall below freezing from November. October is the busiest month, so lodges fill and guides are in demand.

March to May is the flower season. Rhododendrons bloom red, pink and white along the ridge, magnolias flower lower down and nights are milder. The trade-off is haze and afternoon cloud, which often hide the mountains by late morning, and occasional thunderstorms. Start each day early to make the most of the clear hours.

January and February are for experienced winter walkers. Snow can lie deep above Kalipokhri, the jeep track may be blocked and night temperatures drop to -10°C or lower. Views can be superb on clear days. From mid-June to mid-September the park is normally closed to trekkers, and in any case the trail is wet, leech-infested and clouded. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: What the trek costs
paras: Sandakphu is one of the cheapest Himalayan treks to organise yourself with a local guide. The table gives indicative 2025–26 costs. Budget trekkers sharing a guide and staying in dormitory beds can manage on about ₹2,500–3,500 per person a day on the ridge. Packages from Darjeeling operators, including transport, guide, lodges and meals, usually cost ₹12,000–25,000 per person for five to seven days, depending on group size and comfort.

sections.heading: What to pack
paras: The ridge is cold, windy and remote, and lodges supply only basic bedding. Pack for freezing nights in any season, but keep your bag light, because every kilogram is felt on the steep climb from Manebhanjan and the descent to Srikhola. Darjeeling's shops sell and hire most trekking gear if you arrive short of something.
list: Sleeping bag rated to about -5°C in spring and autumn, -10°C in winter, plus a liner.
Down or synthetic insulated jacket, fleece, thermal top and bottom.
Waterproof jacket and trousers, especially in spring.
Broken-in trekking boots with good grip, and light shoes or sandals for the lodges.
Woollen hat, sun cap, gloves, sunglasses and high-factor sunscreen.
Trekking poles for the descent to Srikhola.
Head torch with spare batteries, and a power bank; electricity is limited.
Water bottles and purification tablets or a filter.
Snacks: dry fruit, nuts, chocolate and energy bars.
Basic first-aid kit, personal medicines, blister plasters and oral rehydration salts.
Cash for the whole trip in small notes; there are no ATMs on the ridge.
Original photo ID and a photocopy.

sections.heading: Altitude, safety and the border
paras: Sandakphu is high enough for altitude sickness to be a real, if modest, risk, especially for people who drive up in one day. The three-day walking route helps because it gains height gradually. Common symptoms are headache, nausea, loss of appetite, dizziness and poor sleep. Drink plenty of water, avoid alcohol, walk at a steady pace and tell your guide about any symptoms. If they worsen, the only reliable cure is to go down; Land Rovers can be called up the ridge track in an emergency.

The other hazards are weather and cold. Thick cloud can roll in quickly and hide the trail, so stay with your guide. Ice on the stone path in winter makes the descent slippery, and poles help. Mobile signal is patchy; Indian and Nepali networks come and go along the ridge, so tell someone at home your plans.

The trail weaves between India and Nepal, and in places you sleep on the Nepal side. This is normal and accepted for trekkers on the main route, but keep your ID with you, follow any instructions at border posts and do not take shortcuts into unfamiliar valleys. Travellers with heart or lung conditions should talk to a doctor before the trek.

sections.heading: Getting there and back
paras: Start in Darjeeling, which is 65–70 km and 3–3.5 hours from NJP or Bagdogra. From Darjeeling, shared jeeps run to Manebhanjan from the Chowk Bazar stand through the morning, taking 1–1.5 hours via Ghum and Sukhiapokhri; a reserved car is faster and lets you leave at dawn. Spend the night before in Darjeeling to rest and check kit.

At the end of the trek, Rimbik has shared and reserved jeeps back to Darjeeling, taking 4–5 hours. If you return along the ridge to Manebhanjan instead, jeeps for Darjeeling and Mirik leave from the main road. Plan at least one buffer day before your train or flight from NJP or Bagdogra, in case weather or road conditions delay you.

faqs.q: Is a guide compulsory for the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Yes. Trekkers in Singalila National Park must be accompanied by a licensed guide, hired from the Manebhanjan guide association or arranged through a registered operator. Fees are about ₹1,500–2,000 a day per group, indicative. Groups can share a guide. Rules can be tightened or changed, so check current status before you travel and confirm when you book.

faqs.q: How many days does the Sandakphu trek take?
faqs.a: Allow five days on foot from Manebhanjan and back to Darjeeling via Srikhola and Rimbik, plus a night in Darjeeling at each end. Adding Phalut takes seven days on foot. Some fit trekkers do the climb in two days, but three days to Sandakphu is kinder for altitude and gives better evenings at Tumling and Kalipokhri.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: Moderate. There is no technical climbing, but you walk 5–7 hours on most days, gain about 1,500 m on the way up and lose about 1,700 m on the descent to Srikhola. Fit beginners manage it well with some training. Cold nights, steep stone paths and altitude are the main challenges. Porters can carry heavy bags.

faqs.q: What does the Sandakphu trek cost?
faqs.a: A self-organised trek with a shared guide costs about ₹2,500–3,500 per person per day on the ridge, plus transport from Darjeeling. Packages from Darjeeling operators run about ₹12,000–25,000 per person for five to seven days, depending on group size and lodge standard. Prices are indicative for 2025–26 and rise in October.

Yes. Foreign nationals need a passport with a valid Indian visa, pay a higher park entry fee and must trek with a licensed guide like everyone else. The trail crosses into Nepal in places, and border posts may check documents. No separate Sandakphu permit is needed at the time of writing. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see Everest from Sandakphu?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear mornings Everest, Lhotse and Makalu appear to the west, about 140 km away, alongside the Kangchenjunga range to the north. The best chances are October to mid-December. In spring the view is often hazy by mid-morning. Be outside at sunrise and bring binoculars; your guide will point out each peak.

faqs.q: Where do I stay on the Sandakphu trek?
faqs.a: In simple family lodges and government trekkers' huts at Tumling, Gairibas, Kalipokhri, Sandakphu, Srikhola and Rimbik. Expect shared or private unheated rooms, thick quilts, basic toilets and hot meals by the kitchen fire. Beds cost about ₹400–1,500. Your guide usually books ahead; in October rooms at Sandakphu fill early.

Not for trekkers. Singalila National Park traditionally closes to trekking from mid-June to mid-September for the monsoon. Heavy snow in January and February can also block the trail and the jeep track for days. The best windows are October to mid-December and March to May. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I do Sandakphu without trekking?
faqs.a: Yes. Land Rovers and other permitted four-wheel drives run from Manebhanjan up the ridge track to Sandakphu in about 4–5 hours, for about ₹5,000–7,500 per vehicle one way, indicative. Stay a night at Tumling or Kalipokhri on the way up to help with the altitude, then a night at Sandakphu for the sunrise.
